claim: Old Class 8 book sequence: Mir Jafar protested, Company deposed him and installed Mir Qasim; Mir Qasim lost at Buxar (1764), was driven out, and Mir Jafar was reinstalled
value: NCERT order: Mir Qasim -> Buxar -> Mir Jafar reinstated
source: NCERT, Our Pasts III (Class 8, History), ch. 2 From Trade to Territory; 2nd revised ed. July 2022, reprint 2024-25

claim: Old Class 8 book: the Nawab had to pay Rs 500,000 every month
source: NCERT, Our Pasts III (Class 8, History), ch. 2 From Trade to Territory; 2nd revised ed. July 2022, reprint 2024-25
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [Aitchison Bengal No. VIII (agreement 16 Sept 1764) and No. IX (treaty 20 Feb 1765, Najm-ud-daula)]
note: Amount is right (five lakhs a month towards the war against the Wazir of Oudh). Timing: agreed by Mir Jafar on 16 Sept 1764, i.e. before Buxar, and renewed for Najm-ud-daula in Feb 1765. NCERT's sentence reads as after Buxar

claim: Old Class 8 book: Clive declared 'We must indeed become nawabs ourselves'
source: NCERT, Our Pasts III (Class 8, History), ch. 2 From Trade to Territory; 2nd revised ed. July 2022, reprint 2024-25

claim: Old Class 8 book: in 1765 the Mughal emperor appointed the Company as Diwan of the provinces of Bengal; diwani allowed the Company to use the revenue of Bengal
source: NCERT, Our Pasts III (Class 8, History), ch. 2 From Trade to Territory; 2nd revised ed. July 2022, reprint 2024-25
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [Aitchison Bengal No. X (farman 12 Aug 1765)]

claim: Old Class 8 book: gold flow from Britain 'slowed after Plassey and entirely stopped after the assumption of Diwani'
source: NCERT, Our Pasts III (Class 8, History), ch. 2 From Trade to Territory; 2nd revised ed. July 2022, reprint 2024-25

claim: Old Class 8 book quotes Clive at the hearing: he stood 'astonished at my own moderation'

claim: Black Hole: Holwell's printed account (1758) says 146 prisoners went in on the night of 20 June 1756 and 123 died, i.e. 23 survived
source: J.Z. Holwell, A Genuine Narrative of the Deplorable Deaths of the English Gentlemen ... in the Black-Hole (London, 1758)
page_or_section: opening pages and list of the smothered (p.55)
second_source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [Intro p.xci: 'twenty-three of one hundred and forty-six'; Hill doc.49 p.66: '146 or 150 ... 23']
note: Figures differ between accounts (rows below). Holwell was a survivor and an interested party; the numbers are disputed, treat as contested on screen

claim: Black Hole: Holwell's own letter of 17 July 1756 gives about 165-170 put in and about 16 who came out alive
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
note: Two years before his printed account, the same author gives different numbers. Recorded for the debate, not to be resolved

claim: Black Hole: Captain Mills' narrative says 144 men, women and children were put in and 'upwards of 120' died
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
note: Another survivor's account, different count

claim: Black Hole: another contemporary account (Captain Grant) says 'near 200' were put in and 'not above ten' survived to morning
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents

claim: Black Hole: Cambridge History of India vol. V gives the room as 18 feet by 14 feet 10 inches and says 23 survivors came out
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [Intro p.xc fn: Dr C.R. Wilson found the exact dimensions to be 18 ft by 14 ft 10 in]
note: Dimensions have two agreeing modern sources; the number inside is the disputed part

claim: Black Hole: the English translator's footnote to the Seir Mutaqherin says the event is not known in Bengal, even in Calcutta, and that the Nawab's men only meant to hold prisoners for the night; it gives 131 shut up
source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2
note: This is a translator's note, not the Indian author's text; the author's main text (p.190) says nothing of the room. Treat as one named view. Who the translator was is not stated on the title page I read (catalogues say Haji Mustafa: UNVERIFIED)

claim: Black Hole: J.H. Little (Bengal Past and Present, 1915-16) argued Holwell's story was untrustworthy; H.H. Dodwell answered that the main outlines stand and that the exact number cannot be settled
value: Little: doubt; Dodwell: outline stands, number unknown
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
note: Little's own articles were not reached; Dodwell's summary of them is what I read. Modern university-press treatments (e.g. P. Chatterjee, The Black Hole of Empire, Princeton UP, 2012) were not reachable (see search log)

claim: No NCERT book read teaches the Black Hole; the sources above show its figures and cause are disputed

source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
note: Single source; consistent with Seir's account of Clive's return (Seir 2 p.229)

claim: A treaty and a separate agreement were made with Siraj-ud-daula in February 1757: it restored the Company's privileges and factories, allowed fortification of Calcutta and a mint (siccas at Calcutta), and the Company promised alliance (agreement of 12 Feb 1757, Clive)

source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892

claim: Chandernagore (French) was attacked by Clive on 23 March 1757 and fell
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
page_or_section: Intro p.cxlix-ff; text at 'morning of the 23rd March Clive stormed the French battery'
note: Surrender date not separately read

claim: Treaty with Mir Jafar, 1757 (signed by Clive, Admiral Watson, Drake, Watts), article 4: Rs 1 crore to the Company for its losses and the cost of the forces; art. 5: Rs 50 lakh for English inhabitants of Calcutta; art. 6: Rs 20 lakh for Hindus, Muslims and other subjects; art. 7: Rs 7 lakh for Armenians
as_of: 1757 (dated '15 Ramzan, year 4' of the reign; roughly 3-4 June 1757 by my arithmetic)
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892

claim: What Mir Jafar actually paid: Clive reported the treasury at Murshidabad held about Rs 150 lakh; Jagat Seth fixed that the Company get one half of its demand at once (two-thirds in money, one-third in plate, jewels and goods) and the other half in three equal yearly payments
value: ~150 lakh in treasury; half at once; half over 3 years
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents
page_or_section: doc. 501, Clive to Secret Committee 26 July 1757, p.460
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772 [p.154 (Clive: lands worth GBP 700,000 a year mortgaged for the unpaid part; paid half down, half in about 15 months, as he remembered)]
note: Clive's two accounts differ in how long the second half took (3 years in 1757 letter; 'about 15 months' in 1772 memory). Both are Clive's own words

claim: Clive's own evidence to the 1772 Commons Select Committee: he received about Rs 16 lakh 'clear' as his private donation (Watts told him it would be about 20); Watts about 8, Walsh about 5, Kilpatrick 3-4, Scrafton about 2, Lushington about 0.5, Capt. Grant 1 lakh; his share as Commander-in-Chief about 2 lakh
value: Clive ~16 lakh private (+~2 lakh as C-in-C)
source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772
second_source: John Malcolm, The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, vol. 3 (London, 1836) [vol. 3, text of the Commons resolution of 1773: 2 lakh as Commander-in-Chief, 2 lakh 80,000 as Select Committee member, 16 lakh or more private donation = 20 lakh 80,000, about GBP 234,000]
note: Different totals on purpose: Clive's 1772 words stress the 16; Parliament's 1773 resolution counts all three heads (20.8 lakh). Both recorded; Malcolm is a biographer printing the resolution, original Journal of the House not read

claim: Clive told the Select Committee he himself planned the 'fictitious treaty' to deceive Omichund, who had demanded 5 per cent of the Nawab's treasure and Rs 30 lakh; Admiral Watson's name was signed on it by Lushington on Clive's order
source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772
second_source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [Intro p.clxxxvii-clxxxviii (quotes Clive's evidence and adds Hill's own comment)]
note: Surprising claim; two sources, but Hill quotes the same Commons evidence, so they are not fully independent. Hill adds the view that Clive and the committee 'quieted their consciences'; that is Hill's judgment

claim: Clive's march to Plassey: he left Chandernagore on 13 June 1757, reached Cutwa on 18 June, crossed the river on the evening of 22 June and reached Plassey Grove about 1 am on the 23rd

second_source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [p.149 (reached Plassey at midnight 22-23 June)]

claim: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757

claim: Nawab's army at Plassey per Clive's report: about 15,000 horse, 35,000 foot, and upwards of 40 guns

source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents
page_or_section: doc. 501 p.458; Hill I Intro p.ccii
note: Two English-record figures disagree. Hill does not say where his tally comes from in the text I read

claim: Nawab's side lost about 500 killed at Plassey (Clive), and Siraj-ud-daula fled on a camel
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents
second_source: none independent (Hill repeats Clive)
note: Hill likely repeats Clive's figure; treat as one estimate Treat as Clive's estimate, about 500. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: At Plassey Mir Jafar and Rai Durlabh stood on the English right and did not fight (Hill; Seir). Clive reports he fired on the unsignalling troops to keep them at a distance, and they sent a message after the battle
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
second_source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2; S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents [Seir vol.2 p.231 (Mir Jafar 'contented himself with standing at a distance'); Clive's report p.458 (a large body hovering on the right, 'our friends')]
note: Three accounts, two Indian-side/English-side perspectives, agree on non-participation. Seir adds that Mir Madan fell by a cannon-ball and that Mohan Lal was ordered to retreat Clive (Hill vol. II doc. 501): they gave no signal, he fired 'to make them keep their distance', and they sent a congratulatory message once the battle was over; he does not say he took them for enemy. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: A council of war on 21 June 1757 voted: Clive against immediate action; of the rest, twelve voted against and seven for (Hill)
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772 [p.149 and 154: Clive in 1772 first said all but Coote and Grant voted against; later told the committee he had made a mistake about the number]
note: Records vs Clive's own 15-year-old memory; teach the record (Hill) and the fact that Clive corrected himself

claim: Siraj-ud-daula was captured and put to death at Murshidabad around 2 July 1757 on the order of Mir Jafar's son Miran, 'without the father's knowledge' (as Clive reported it)
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772; IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar [Commons p.150 (Clive's 1772 words: put to death by Miran, 'it is said, without the Father's knowledge'); IGNOU Unit 8 sec 8.3.1: murdered by order of Mir Jafar's son Miran]
note: 'Without the father's knowledge' is Clive's report of what he was told; Seir not checked on this point

claim: Mir Jafar was installed as Nawab: Clive's report says he entered Murshidabad on the 29th with 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys and led Mir Jafar to the musnud; Hill's narrative puts the entry on 28 June with 100 King's troops, grenadiers and 500 sepoys
source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. II (Indian Records Series, 1905), documents
second_source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [Intro p.cci-ccii]
note: Small date and troop-number difference between Clive's letter and Hill's retelling; if the date is used on screen say 'late June'

claim: Cambridge History V's judgment on Plassey: Clive found Mir Jafar would stand neutral; Clive reached Plassey with about 3,000 men facing some 50,000 and could not be certain of Mir Jafar
value: Dodwell (1929): odds large on paper, Mir Jafar uncertain
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar [sec 8.3.1: Plassey's result 'decided before the battle was fought']
note: Both are named secondary views: Dodwell (CUP, 1929) and IGNOU's unit (unattributed author). A modern CUP view (P.J. Marshall, 1987) was not reachable

claim: Seir Mutaqherin (Indian contemporary): Siraj's court was divided; Rajah Durlabh Ram at Plassey made a private agreement with the English; Siraj pleaded with Mir Jafar and was refused; the Nawab's army dispersed and he fled
value: Indian chronicler's view of the defection
source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2
second_source: S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [Intro p.cc-cci]
note: Seir's author wrote around 1781-82 and was connected to the Patna court; the translation adds footnotes. His moral comments ('treason') are his, not evidence of fact

claim: In 1759 a Dutch force came from Batavia; Clive attacked and defeated it; a convention (Dec 1757) and agreement (Aug 1760) with the Dutch are in the treaty collection
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
page_or_section: Bengal narrative p.3 and Nos. IV-V
note: Optional; belongs to the 'rivals removed' point (French 1757, Dutch 1759)

claim: Mir Kasim, Mir Jafar's son-in-law, replaced him by treaty of 27 September 1760; the Company got Bardwan (Burdwan), Midnapur and Chittagong to pay for its army
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
second_source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar; H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [IGNOU sec 8.3.3; CHI V ch. IX]
note: Mir Jafar kept his dignities in the treaty (art. 1) - the instrument is a transfer of power inside the family

claim: Clive left India for England on 25 February 1760, handing the chair to Holwell
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)

claim: Mir Kasim moved his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr (Munger) in Bihar, away from Calcutta
source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar
second_source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [p.172 ('Mongir, where he had established his capital')]

claim: Dispute under Mir Kasim: the Company's servants traded duty-free in salt, betel, tobacco and other goods in the internal trade, which the nawab said was never allowed; Vansittart made an agreement with him at the end of 1762 (English pay 9 per cent where Indian merchants paid 40 on salt to Patna) which the Calcutta council rejected; Mir Kasim then resolved to abolish duties
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar; S.C. Hill (ed.), Bengal in 1756-57, vol. I (Indian Records Series, Govt of Bengal, 1905), Introduction and documents [IGNOU sec 8.3.3 (dustak misuse); Hill I Intro p.lv (earlier abuse of dastaks)]
note: Dodwell's account (1929) of the internal-trade dispute; he argues the interests of English and nawab were 'irreconcilable'. Primary letters (Vansittart's narrative) not read

claim: War of 1763: Major Adams took the field on 10 June 1763 with 1,100 Europeans and 4,000 sepoys against Mir Kasim's 15,000-20,000; Mir Kasim lost four battles, put English prisoners to death at Patna, and fled to Oudh
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [Bengal narrative p.4 (murder of English prisoners; flight to Oudh and Delhi; died in poverty 1777)]
note: Numbers are Dodwell's, source of his figures not examined. Number of prisoners killed at Patna not read (UNVERIFIED if needed)

claim: Mir Jafar was restored by treaty of 10 July 1763: the Company would depose Mir Kasim; Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong stayed with the Company; English trade duty-free except a duty on salt (printed as 24, read by Dodwell as 2.5 per cent); Mir Kasim's two-year duty exemption for all merchants cancelled; Mir Jafar to keep 12,000 horse and 12,000 foot, receive an English resident, and pay Rs 30 lakh for the Company's war costs
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
second_source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [p.173-174 (2.5 per cent salt duty; resident)]
note: OCR of the salt duty reads '24 per cent'; Dodwell gives 2.5 per cent. Page image not viewed - treat the exact rate as unverified, the other terms as read

claim: Mir Jafar died in January 1765 and was succeeded by his son Najm-ud-daula; the new treaty (executed 20 Feb 1765) put defence wholly in Company hands and required a deputy (Naib Subah, Muhammad Reza Khan) not removable without Company consent
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
page_or_section: Bengal narrative p.4; No. IX p.53-56
second_source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar [sec 8.3.4]
note: IGNOU says Najm-ud-daula was minor and the Company chose the deputy; Aitchison's treaty text names Muhammad Reza Khan as the Naib Subah

claim: Battle of Buxar (Baksar): Major Hector Munro defeated the army of Shuja-ud-daula (Wazir of Oudh), Mir Kasim and Shah Alam II; Cambridge History gives the date as 22 October 1764
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772 [p.167 (Munro's evidence: 'Upon the 22d of October we arrived at Buxar'; attack planned 23rd; the action began about 9 am after reconnoitring on the morning of the 23rd)]
note: DATE CONFLICT: 22 Oct (Dodwell) vs 23 Oct (Munro's own account read in sequence). Munro's wording does not print 'battle on the 23rd' in one sentence - I read it from the order of events on p.167 (page image viewed). Settle with a day-by-day source (Munro's dispatch, Fort William-India House Correspondence)

claim: Buxar strength per Munro: 857 Europeans, 5,297 sepoys, 918 'black cavalry' = 7,072 men and 20 field pieces; enemy reported 60,000 but Munro was sure it was 'not less than 40,000'
source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772
second_source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2 [vol.2 p.563-568 (no head-count; 'eight regiments of Talingas'; a translator's note says 5-6,000 died on the field and 10,000+ in the mire)]
note: RANGE and single-eyewitness: figures are Munro's testimony in 1772 recalled from memory/papers. Treat as 'about 7,000 against several times as many'

claim: Buxar losses per Munro: killed and wounded 847 on the Company side (Europeans 34 killed, 49 wounded; sepoys 205 killed, 414 wounded, 85 missing); enemy at least 2,000 killed on the field plus about 2,000 drowned; 133 guns captured
source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772
second_source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2 [vol.2 p.567-568 and note 300 (translator: 5-6,000 killed, 10,000+ in the mire)]
note: CONFLICT in enemy losses: Munro 4,000 vs translator's note 15,000+. Neither is a count

claim: Munro's account: Shuja-ud-daula offered, through his minister Beni Bahadur, Rs 25 lakh for the Company's war expenses, Rs 25 lakh for the army and Rs 8 lakh for Munro himself, if the Company dropped the demand to hand over Mir Kasim and Sumro; Munro refused
source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772
note: Single source (Munro's own testimony). Include only if the episode needs it

claim: Seir Mutaqherin: Shah Alam II was in Shuja-ud-daula's camp but left before the battle and wrote to Munro after it; Seir says Shuja freed Mir Qasim the day before the battle
source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint R. Cambray, 1902), vol. 2
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772 [p.168 (Munro: the 'Mogul' wrote after the battle saying he had left the Vizier the night before)]
note: Seir's claim that Shuja freed Mir Qasim on the eve is Seir's alone; not checked elsewhere

claim: 12 August 1765, Allahabad: Emperor Shah Alam II's farman grants the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa 'from the beginning of the Fussul Rubby of the Bengal year 1172', as a free gift, 'from generation to generation', on condition the Company stands security for Rs 26 lakh a year as the royal revenue (paid from the nawab) and that after paying 26 lakh and the expenses of the nizamat, what remains goes to the Company
value: Diwani: Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; 26 lakh a year to the emperor; surplus to the Company
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
second_source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar; H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [IGNOU sec 8.3.4; CHI V p.176-177]
note: The farman is the instrument; 'Treaty of Allahabad' in the textbooks usually means this and the 16 Aug treaty together

claim: Agreement of 19 Aug 1765: the nawab agreed to pay the emperor Rs 26 lakh a year (Rs 2,16,666-10-9 a month, via Patna to Raja Shitab Rai); the Company guaranteed it; Najaf Khan to get Rs 2 lakh a year
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892

claim: Nizamat allowance fixed on 30 Sept 1765: Rs 53,86,131 sicca a year (of which Rs 17,78,854 for the nawab's household and Rs 36,07,277 for troops for his state); the allowance was cut to Rs 41,86,131 (1766), Rs 31,81,991 (1770) and Rs 16 lakh (1772)
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892
page_or_section: Bengal No. X article 4 p.60-61; narrative p.4-5
note: Shows who got what: emperor 26 lakh, nawab 53.86 lakh, the Company the remainder

claim: Treaty with Shuja-ud-daula, 16 August 1765 (Allahabad): perpetual peace; he must not shelter Mir Kasim or Sumro; Shah Alam keeps Kora and part of Allahabad province; Shuja pays the Company Rs 50 lakh (12 lakh cash plus 8 lakh jewels at signing, 5 lakh a month later, 25 lakh in monthly instalments over 13 months); duty-free trade for the Company in his dominions; Balwant Singh keeps Benares-Ghazipur zamindari
value: 50 lakh; Kora and Allahabad to the emperor
source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (UP, Oudh, Bengal, Central Provinces), revised to 1 June 1906, Calcutta 1909, Part II Oudh
second_source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929) [p.176 (Clive restored Shuja's dominions except Allahabad, for 50 lakh; Allahabad to the emperor)]
note: The Seir also records Clive going to Allahabad (vol. 3 p.8-9)

claim: The 1765 settlement as understood by Dodwell (1929): Clive demanded the diwani from the emperor 'as the price of Allahabad', intending full control of finance without avowed sovereignty, which might trouble neither Parliament nor the French and Dutch
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
note: Dodwell's reading of motive; present as his view. 'Power was separated from responsibility' is his judgment of the plan

claim: Seir Mutaqherin on the grant: Clive asked at Allahabad that the Company be invested with the Divanship of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; the emperor and the Wazir, 'overawed', granted it reluctantly; the Seir gives the yearly tribute as twenty-four lakhs
source: Seir Mutaqherin by Ghulam Husain Khan (English translation 1789; Calcutta reprint), vol. 3
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [No. X (26 lakh)]
note: CONFLICT: 24 lakh (Seir) vs 26 lakh (farman and agreement). The farman text wins for what was signed; the Seir shows how an Indian contemporary understood it

claim: Diwani is the office of revenue (the 'Khalsa'); the nawab kept the nizamat (military and policing powers) in form, and the Company took defence by the Feb 1765 treaty. IGNOU says defence, law and order and justice stayed with the nawabs
source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [No. IX (Feb 1765) and No. X article 4]
note: The farman text itself speaks of the diwani revenue; it does not mention judicial powers. Whether 'civil justice' was part of diwani needs a dedicated source (Regulating Act / HIS-33)

claim: Parliament 1773 resolutions on Clive: he obtained at least Rs 20 lakh 80,000 (2 + 2.8 + '16 lacs or more') (about GBP 234,000) at the time of Mir Jafar's installation; a motion that he abused his powers was rejected; the House unanimously resolved he 'did render great and meritorious services to his country'
source: John Malcolm, The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, vol. 3 (London, 1836)
page_or_section: vol. 3, narrative of the 1773 debate (end of Parliament section)
note: Single source: Malcolm (1836), a sympathetic biographer, printing the resolutions. The Journal of the House was not reached. NCERT's 'acquitted' is not the language of the resolutions Single secondary source: Malcolm printing the resolutions; Journal of the House not read. Third head is '16 lacs or more', so Rs 20.8 lakh is a floor. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: Clive's jagir was worth GBP 30,000 a year in 1765
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
second_source: Reports from Committees of the House of Commons, vol. III (reprinted by order of the House): First Report from the Select Committee on the East India Company, 1772 [p.154-155 (jagir discussion)]
note: Value is Dodwell's; origin of the jagir (quit-rent of Calcutta lands) is in Aitchison Bengal narrative p.3 'about three lakhs per annum'

claim: Mir Jafar left Clive a legacy of GBP 70,000 in 1765, which Clive paid into the Company's treasury in 1766 to support disabled soldiers (the Clive Fund)
source: John Malcolm, The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, vol. 3 (London, 1836)
note: Single secondary source (Malcolm). Optional detail

claim: IGNOU Unit 8 says Mir Jafar paid out about Rs 1,750,000 in presents and compensation to the British
source: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of India (BHIC), Unit 8 The British in Eastern India up to Buxar
second_source: C.U. Aitchison, Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads, vol. I (Bengal Presidency etc.), Calcutta: Govt of India, 1892 [No. III: stipulated total Rs 1.77 crore (1,77,00,000)]
note: Probable slip in the IGNOU text (17.5 lakh vs treaty total 177 lakh, a factor of ten). Do not quote IGNOU's figure; use the treaty articles and Clive's report

claim: New NCERT: the 1770-72 Bengal famine killed 'nearly one-third' of the population, about 10 million
source: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 1, ch. 4 The Colonial Era in India; 1st ed. July 2025, reprint March 2026 (marked 2026-27)

claim: New NCERT (drain): Brooks Adams (1895) said Bengal plunder arrived in London soon after Plassey; Utsa Patnaik's estimate for 1765-1938 is 45 trillion US dollars at today's value, about 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP
source: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 1, ch. 4 The Colonial Era in India; 1st ed. July 2025, reprint March 2026 (marked 2026-27)

claim: The Regulating Act of 1773, Pitt's India Act (1784) and diarchy/dual government belong to a later episode
source: H.H. Dodwell (ed. and author of chs VII-IX), The Cambridge History of India, vol. V, British India 1497-1858 (Cambridge University Press, 1929)
note: HIS-33 covers them. HIS-30 stops when the Company holds the diwani (1765) and shows how the 'no-responsibility' problem arises
